newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Star of Vietnam's reforms seeks state partner.
newsitem.headline: Star of Vietnam's reforms seeks state partner.

text.p: Vietnam's Huy Hoang company, a private-sector flagship of the communist country's decade-old market reform drive, said on Monday it was discussing plans to go into partnership with a state enterprise.

An official with the Ho Chi Minh City-based firm told Reuters that local Communist Party authorities had approved a proposal for the conglomerate to examine ways of working together with a state company.
"It's to implement the party policy of developing a state capitalist economic sector by using management skills and capital from private business," said the official, who declined to be identified.
He said the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee was expected to come up with a list of prospective partners soon.
Huy Hoang, a garment manufacturer with interests in construction, real estate and other areas, was founded in 1990 by a former Communist Party member, Le Van Kiem, with initial capital of $1 million.
Its fortunes are seen as having paralleled those of Kiem, who flaunted his personal wealth with diamond-encrusted watches and a fleet of Mercedes and Rolls-Royce cars.

Officials at the firm declined to discuss the reasons behind the move. But the news follows signs of growing problems among domestic firms once seen as riding the crest of market reform policies which were introduced in the late 1980s.

In January this year, four people were sentenced to death and others were jailed for involvement in a corruption scandal at Tamexco -- a leading Ho Chi Minh City trading firm with links to the ruling Communist Party.

Further troubles surfaced last month when the heads of Minh Phung and Epco -- two major private sector companies -- were arrested for alleged involvement in a property scam which has left domestic banks sitting on a mountain of bad debt.
Industry sources said Huy Hoang's decision was a reaction to these developments.

"The Tamexco trial and these arrests have caused real panic among people in the private sector," said one analyst. "It (Huy Hoang's decision) is a way of seeking state protection, to go the safe way."
Vietnam's market reform policies were introduced after the failure of its Soviet-style, command-led system.

The result was an economic lift-off and social changes which have seen a transformation of the country's status from that of a virtual pariah state into an increasingly respected member of the international community.
But the growth of corruption, consumerism and social vice has led to questioning of the merits of the reforms and a political emphasis on ensuring the dominance of the lumbering state sector.

Economists said Huy Hoang's decision would buy it protection from the kind of problems being experienced by some other private firms, but warned that going into business with a state firm would present the company with new risks.
"The problem is...that if two sick guys are merging together, then the sickness will be developing," said a Hanoi academic. "Then it may appear in a different form."
